transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-23
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Seacliff VP Eng), Samir Khan (CTO), Priya Desai (ML Infra)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on hosting path.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, with Diego our solutions engineer, and you all?
[00:08] Lena (Seacliff): Hi Maya, hi Diego — Lena here. We appreciate the time. We wanted to cover latency and throughput profiling — basically figure out whether hosted makes sense or if we need dedicated capacity for predictable p95s.
[00:21] Diego (Redwood): Great — quick agenda: understand your traffic patterns, p95 targets, streaming needs, and any compliance constraints. Then we can propose benchmark windows and what to measure.
[00:30] Samir (Seacliff): Quick context: Seacliff runs a chat assist feature for our enterprise docs product. Typical sessions are 150-400 tokens generated, sometimes up to 2k for long transcripts. Peak concurrency around 220 active users during business hours, but we have bursts to ~1,400 concurrent users during batch notifications.
[00:49] Priya (Seacliff): Most traffic is streaming; clients expect sub-300ms per-chunk latency so progressive rendering. Our p95 goal end-to-end is 600ms for each user token at our 95th percentile during steady-state. For spikes we want graceful degradation — not full failures.
[01:10] Diego (Redwood): Ok, that's helpful. Two immediate knobs: 1) Serving mode — hosted shared pools vs dedicated GPU pools; 2) batching and prefix/KV caching to lower token cost and end-to-end latency.
[01:23] Lena: Can you quantify differences? Like p95 on hosted for streaming vs dedicated for same model?
[01:29] Diego: Rough ballpark — on a 70B-ish open model with streaming optimized runtime we often see p95 token latencies in hosted of ~300–600ms depending on seq length and batching; for dedicated, with pinned capacity and tuned autoscaling, p95 can tighten to ~150–300ms and be much more predictable under load. But these numbers vary a lot with token/sec and concurrency.
[01:50] Samir: That delta is pretty big. Our main worry is the burst to 1.4k — how does Redwood handle that? Will hosted throttle?
[01:58] Maya: There are a few patterns — with hosted we have multi-tier routing: try low-latency pools first, then fallback to cheaper or quantized variants if necessary. For predictable SLAs and reserved throughput you'd want Dedicated. Dedicated gives you committed GPU lanes; autoscaling policies can give headroom for bursts but you plan cost vs reserve.
[02:18] Priya: What about cold starts for KV cache? If user comes back in a session, we rely on KV cache for attention states — is that persisted across requests for streaming?
[02:26] Diego: We maintain KV cache per-request session in the runtime and can optionally enable prefix caching. For longer sessions we recommend sticky routing or session affinity in Dedicated mode. In hosted we do support cache but eviction policies can make tail latencies inconsistent.
[02:44] Lena: Security — we need SOC2, SSO + SAML, KMS integration, and audit logs retained for 1 year. Does Redwood Hosted support all of that?
[02:53] Maya: Hosted supports SOC2 and SSO, and SOC2 artifacts are available via our compliance pack. KMS for hosted is available with customer-managed keys in our higher tiers; Private or Dedicated gives you tighter network isolation and customer-controlled KMS/HSM. We can send the compliance snapshot.
[03:10] Samir: Cost question — we run roughly 12M tokens/day currently. Any heuristics on hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved cost?
[03:18] Diego: Hosted is simple usage-based — good for ramping and dev. Dedicated is best when your steady-state token volumes are high and predictability matters — unit cost often drops materially after factoring reserved capacity and batching. We'll send a cost model showing thresholds.
[03:33] Priya: On model variants — if you fallback to a quantized model during bursts, how much quality drop do we expect? We have regulated customers.
[03:41] Diego: Quality delta depends on quantization and the model family. For many workloads, 4-bit quantization with Redwood-verified kernels introduces negligible quality regressions for classification or short summarization, but for long form legal text you may see subtle changes. We recommend running side-by-side warns.
[03:58] Lena: Let's talk benchmarks — what do you need from us to reproduce realistic traffic?
[04:04] Diego: Ideally: 1) token/sec distribution and per-session length histogram, 2) concurrency time-of-day heatmap, 3) sample prompt set and desired p95 target, 4) any network egress constraints or VPC needs. We'll provide a harness that runs streaming and non-streaming tests and reports p50/p95/p99 latencies, token/sec, and cost.
[04:29] Samir: We can provide traces, Priya will send them. For benchmarks can you simulate stateful sessions with KV cache warmup?
[04:36] Diego: Yes, we can replay sessions with KV cache warm starts; for Dedicated we can test sticky routing and autoscale.
[04:44] Priya: One more thing — we require audit logs for model invocations tied to user ids. Hosted logs are ok as long as they can be forwarded to our SIEM.
[04:53] Maya: That's supported — hosted can stream logs and we have options to forward to customer endpoints or S3. For Private deployments you manage logs entirely.
[05:02] [short pause, rustling papers]
[05:10] Lena: Timeline: we're deciding by mid-April. We'll likely want a pilot through June.
[05:16] Maya: Great — that aligns. We'll propose a benchmark slot and send pricing options.
[05:21] Samir: Regarding fallback policies: can Redwood route per-request to different model sizes (e.g., 70B -> 13B) to keep latency? How transparent is that to the app?
[05:30] Diego: Yes, policy-based routing is available. We can specify latency-first or cost-first; for latency we prefer smaller unquantized models or same-size quantized variants. The runtime can attach metadata to responses so the app knows which variant served the call. Small transcription caveat: sometimes the response header names in the SDK differs across language SDKs.
[05:48] Priya: We do need per-token cost breakdowns for compliance billing.
[05:52] Maya: Console shows token-level cost, model breakdown, and per-route breakdown. We can grant a read-only view for your finance team.
[05:59] [06:00] Diego: Quick technical aside — when measuring p95 for streaming, we recommend measuring the time from first byte to last token arrival and also per-chunk latency for user perceived latency. Network jitter plays a big role; for accurate benching provide an egress point close to your region.
[06:18] Samir: Do you support colocated endpoints in our cloud region?
[06:21] Maya: For Hosted we have region coverage in NA/EU and some APAC — for strict colocation or private control plane you'd use Redwood Private or a Dedicated VPC deployment.
[06:31] Lena: Could you outline what a Dedicated onboarding looks like? Downtime, migrations, config?
[06:37] Diego: Dedicated onboarding: we provision GPU pools, set autoscaling targets, configure model variants and caching policies, and run soak tests. Migration is typically DNS cutover for endpoints; downtime is minimal if you plan a rolling migration. We'll also set up monitoring and tracing hooks.
[06:53] Priya: For the benchmark, we want to test the following scenarios: steady-state 220 concurrency with 400 token outputs, high-traffic burst 1.4k concurrency, and long-session sequences ~2k tokens with many KV cache reuses.
[07:07] Diego: Perfect. We'll craft three scenarios and a combined mixed-workload. We'll run hosted baseline and dedicated tuned tests.
[07:15] Samir: Any limit on streaming chunk size? Our SDK uses 64-token chunks.
[07:20] Diego: 64-token chunks are fine. Runtime supports variable chunk sizes, but smaller chunks mean more RPCs; that's a tradeoff. We can test client chunking strategies as part of bench.
[07:30] Lena: SLA question: if we go hosted and need enterprise SLA, can we get 99.9% uptime and p95 guarantees?
[07:36] Maya: Hosted has product-level SLAs at enterprise tiers; for hard p95 latency SLOs, Dedicated is easier to guarantee because you control the capacity. For hosted we offer latency targets as guidance and fallbacks, but we don't typically include hard latency SLOs in shared pools.
[07:51] Priya: We have regulatory customers in EU — can data stay in-region?
[07:55] Maya: Yes, we support region pinning for model serving and data residency; Private gives the most guarantees. We'll include region availability matrix.
[08:03] [small cross-talk]
[08:10] Samir: Let's cover observability — we need per-route traces, token-level breakdown, and event sampling.
[08:17] Diego: Redwood Console provides per-route dashboards, traces, and latency by token bucket. We can emit spans to your tracing backend (Jaeger/Datadog).
[08:27] Lena: Any integration work required for our infra team?
[08:30] Maya: For hosted, minimal — API keys and optional VPC peering for private endpoints. For Dedicated/Private there's more infra work — VPC setup, KMS keys, and network configs. Diego can provide a runbook.
[08:44] Priya: Security scanning — do you have pen-test reports and certs?
[08:47] Maya: Yes, we'll include pen test summaries and SOC2 Type II.
[08:52] [09:00] Diego: Ok, quick recap and immediate asks: Priya to send traffic traces; Maya will send hosted vs dedicated cost sheet and compliance docs; Diego to send benchmark plan. We'll propose benchmark dates next week.
[09:13] Lena: Sounds good. Anything else?
[09:16] Samir: One more nit — tokenization differences across models change token counts; do you normalize cost per model?
[09:23] Diego: We'll show model-specific tokenization and an apples-to-apples conversion in the cost model. Also plan for model rollouts and A/B to validate quality.
[09:34] Priya: OK, thanks.
[09:36] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll send materials and follow up with proposed bench times.
[09:41] [meeting end]

Notes on transcription quality: some acronyms and product names may be misrecognized (e.g., "Redwood Private" transcribed as "Redwood Privet"), occasional overlap in speaker labels.

Bench plan (short):
- Scenario A: steady-state: 220 concurrent, 400-token outputs, streaming chunks 64 tokens, measure p50/p95/p99, cost/req.
- Scenario B: burst: ramp to 1.4k concurrent sustained for 3 minutes, observe fallbacks and throttles.
- Scenario C: long sessions: 2k tokens, KV cache warm-start vs cold start.
- Compare Hosted baseline -> Dedicated tuned -> Dedicated with sticky sessions + KV caching.

Delivered artefacts: request for traces, compliance pack, hosting cost matrix.
